meta.title: Multi-objective design: Pareto fronts for an anti-alias filter
meta.tools: Enumerated design space (filter family × order × cutoff), Pareto-dominance filtering, weighted-sum vs ε-constraint scalarisation, detection of non-convex front regions
meta.summary: Choose an anti-aliasing filter with three competing goals — stopband attenuation, passband droop and group-delay distortion (plus component count via order) — compute the Pareto front of 2,000 candidate designs, and show that weighted-sum optimisation misses Pareto-optimal designs where the front is non-convex.
meta.problem: 'Best filter' has no meaning with several objectives. What does the set of reasonable choices look like, and which optimisation methods can find all of them?
meta.theory:
A design is Pareto-optimal if no other design is at least as good in every objective and strictly better in one. Minimising a weighted sum Σw_iJ_i finds only designs on the *convex hull* of the front; the ε-constraint method
(minimise J₁ subject to J₂ ≤ ε) reaches every Pareto point. Filter families trade differently: Bessel = low delay distortion, poor selectivity; Chebyshev/elliptic = sharp, distorting; Butterworth in between.
meta.method:
Analog prototypes: Butterworth, Bessel, Chebyshev I (0.5 dB), elliptic (0.5 dB/60 dB), orders 2–8, cutoff 0.5–1.5 × passband edge (fp = 20 kHz, stopband from 30 kHz). Objectives: J₁ = −(min attenuation beyond 30 kHz), J₂ = droop at 20 kHz, J₃ = group-delay
variation over 0–20 kHz (µs). Pareto front in (J₁, J₃) at fixed max droop; weighted sums for 200 weights vs ε-constraint sweep.
meta.track: Applied Mathematics — 218 projects in electrical engineering

rows.quantity: ε-constraint sweep reaches every Pareto point (fraction)
